items.title: The Seven Stations of Consciousness, Sorted by Uniformity of Body and Outlook Across the Cosmos

items.zh: 又有七種諸有情類受生處所，於彼處所受生有情，諸識現前相續而住。於三界中，唯除惡趣、無想有情，及非想非非想處。由惡趣中，極可厭故，不立識住；無想有情，一向轉識不現行故，不立識住；非想非非想處，行與不行不決定故，不立識住。身異類故名種種身，想異類故名種種想。當知與此相違，名一種身、一種想。
items.en: There are also seven places of rebirth for sentient beings, in which consciousness abides, manifest and continuous, once reborn there. Within the three realms, only the evil destinies, beings without perception, and the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception are excluded. Because the evil destinies are utterly repugnant, a station of consciousness is not established there; because beings without perception have consciousness's active forms entirely absent, a station is not established there; and because the sphere of neither perception nor non-perception is undetermined between having and lacking mental activity, a station is not established there. Where bodies differ in kind, this is called manifold body; where conceptions differ in kind, this is called manifold conception. Know that the reverse of this is called uniform body and uniform conception.

items.zh: 梵世已下，身形異類，所生身形種種色相有差別故。於梵世中初受生時，彼諸梵眾咸作是念：我等皆是大梵所生。爾時梵王亦作是念：是諸梵眾皆吾所生。如是彼想非有異類。第二靜慮已上一切諸天，身光等照故，名一種身。光音天眾先後生者，由覩梵世猛焰燒然，爾時便有怖不怖想；是故於彼有異類想。
items.en: Below the Brahmā world, bodily forms are of different kinds, because the bodies born there differ in their many appearances. In the Brahmā world, when they are first born, the Brahmā gods all think: 'We were all born of the Great Brahmā.' And the Brahmā king also thinks: 'These Brahmā gods were all born of me.' Thus their perception is not of different kinds. All the gods from the second dhyāna upwards are called uniform in body, because the light of their bodies shines equally. Among the gods of Radiant Light, those born earlier and later, seeing the Brahmā world consumed by raging flames, have perceptions of fear and of no fear; so they have perceptions of different kinds.

items.title: Seven Latent Afflictions Spanning the Three Realms, and Seven Faults That Mark a Teaching as Wrongly Taught

items.zh: 又諸有情有七種麁重，遍攝一切煩惱品麁重。謂劣界貪、瞋品麁重，中界妙界貪品麁重，劣中妙界慢、無明、見、疑品麁重。又於外道惡說法律中、當知有七種過失。謂解過失、行過失、依止過失、思惟過失、功用過失、增上心過失、增上慧過失。彼諸外道，雖少於法聽聞受持，而常隨順四顛倒故，凡興言論，專為毀他免脫徵難，為勝利故，其所生解皆有過失。所受禁戒，邪範邪命所攝受故，不能令自得出離故，亦有過失。所事師友，唯能宣說顛倒道故，亦有過失。所有思惟，邪求出離損壞心故，亦有過失。所有功用，離方便故，亦有過失。彼增上心，忘念、愛、慢及與無明、疑上靜慮之所攝故，亦有過失。彼增上慧，六十二見所損壞故，亦有過失。與此相違，當知善說法律中，亦有七種無過失事。
items.en: Sentient beings also have seven kinds of coarse latent weight, comprehending the entirety of every class of affliction: the coarse weight of craving and hostility in the inferior realm; the coarse weight of craving in the middle and sublime realms; and the coarse weight of conceit, ignorance, view, and doubt across the inferior, middle, and sublime realms alike. In the wrongly-taught doctrine and discipline of non-Buddhist teachers, know there are seven faults: the fault of understanding, the fault of conduct, the fault of reliance, the fault of reflection, the fault of application, the fault of the higher mind, and the fault of higher wisdom. The reverse of this — know that the well-taught doctrine and discipline likewise has seven faultless qualities.

items.title: The Seven Ways a Monastic Community Resolves Its Own Disputes — the Source Text Concludes

items.zh: 又有七法，令諸苾芻所起違犯諍事止息。餘如攝事分中當說。當知此中，有七種違犯諍事。一、開悟現前犯諍事，二、開悟過去失念犯諍事，三、開悟不自在犯諍事，四、尋思犯諍事，五、決擇犯諍事，六、自悔犯諍事，七、忍愧建立二眾展轉舉罪諍事。
items.en: There are also seven things that bring disputes arising from a violation among monks to rest — the rest will be explained in the Compendium of Topics. Know that there are seven kinds of dispute over a violation: first, the dispute over a violation to be clarified face to face; second, the dispute over a violation, forgotten through lapse of memory, to be clarified; third, the dispute over a violation committed while not in control of oneself, to be clarified; fourth, the dispute over a violation requiring investigation; fifth, the dispute over a violation requiring a decision; sixth, the dispute over a violation one confesses oneself; and seventh, the dispute in which two factions, set up through patience and a sense of shame, raise charges against one another.

blocks.text: The last reading of fascicle 14, and the end of "inner wisdom". It closes, fittingly, with the seven methods by which a monastic community settles its own disputes: the whole long analysis of mind and path ends in the practical work of living together peacefully.

Beings are sorted by uniformity of body and outlook: manifold body and manifold conception (humans and some gods); manifold body and uniform conception; uniform body and manifold conception; uniform body and uniform conception; and the first three formless spheres. The peak of existence is excluded because, Master Cháng Bǎi explains, its beings lack coarse perception yet are not wholly without it; its activity is "undetermined".

For "manifold body, uniform conception", Master Cháng Bǎi tells again the story of Great Brahmā at the beginning of the eon (Day 10): lonely, he wished for company; beings arrived; he thought he had made them, and they thought so too. Different bodies, one mistaken idea.

Seven latent afflictions span the three realms: sensual craving, hostility, craving for existence, conceit, ignorance, views, and doubt. In the form and formless realms there is craving but no hostility. Master Cháng Bǎi: "their virtue is lofty, their minds turn inward; the coarse weight of hostility is gone", though the subtle weight of craving remains.

subs.head: Seven faults of a wrong teaching

blocks.text: A teaching is wrongly taught when it has seven faults; the treatise lists them as marks of non-Buddhist teaching, and they serve as a checklist for any teaching.

The **seven methods of settling disputes** (七滅諍法), from the monastic code: settlement in the presence of the parties, by recollection, by recognition of past insanity, by confession, by majority decision, by investigating the offender's character, and by "covering over with grass" (mutual forgiveness when both sides have erred). Venerable Miào Jìng on the fifth: invite a monk learned in the Vinaya to decide.
The treatise says the rest is "explained in the *Compendium of Topics*" (攝事分). Ru-Yi's English names the *Compendium of Ascertainments*; both teachers read the *Compendium of Topics*.

Fascicles 13 and 14 have set out "inner wisdom", the first of the five sciences a practitioner learns by hearing: the three divisions of scripture; the key terms of the Śrāvakayāna and Mahāyāna, including the three natures; ten principles; and the teachings arranged by number. It is, in effect, a syllabus. Fascicle 15 turns to the other four sciences: medicine, logic, linguistics, and the practical arts.

quiz.q: Neither-perception-nor-non-perception is excluded because activity there is "undetermined." How does Master Cháng Bǎi explain?
options: beings there lack coarse perception yet aren't wholly without it; the thought is subtle and undetermined, without distinct consciousness
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: in that sphere beings have no coarse perception, yet are not wholly without it; the thought is very subtle and undetermined, with no distinct consciousness. Venerable Miào Jìng: consciousness delights in perception, but there it is dim.

quiz.q: For "manifold body, uniform conception," what example does Master Cháng Bǎi give?
options: at the eon's start, Great Brahmā, lonely, wished for company, and beings dying in the second dhyāna came as his retinue
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: at the eon's beginning, Great Brahmā, newly born and lonely, wished for company; at that thought, beings dying in the second dhyāna came as his retinue and ministers. f14 omits these two glosses.

quiz.q: Among the seven latencies, the middle and sublime realms have craving but no hostility. Why, per Master Cháng Bǎi?
options: beings there are virtuous, their minds turned inward, so hostility's coarse weight is gone, though craving's seeds remain heavy
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Their virtue is lofty, their minds turn inward, not outward; the coarse weight of hostility is gone, but the seeds of craving remain heavy." Venerable Miào Jìng: no one there provokes anyone.

quiz.q: For the fifth, "a dispute settled by decision," how do the two teachers describe the method?
options: Miào Jìng: invite a monk learned in the Vinaya to judge; Cháng Bǎi says in one place a majority vote by tally-sticks, elsewhere also a learned monk
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: one must invite a monk who knows the Vinaya well to decide whether it is an offence. Master Cháng Bǎi first describes a majority vote by tally-sticks, later a discerning monk deciding. The note takes only the vote.
